Annual Meetings

Afternoon Session - 1995 Meeting

Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger cover the "real" advantage of being rich, whether they're looking for international acquisitions, the secret to avoiding lawsuits, and what business schools really should be teaching.

Wed, Nov 28 2018 • 3:43 PM EST
Key Chapters —
  1. 5. Buffett on the "real" advantage of being rich
  2. 11. When a company's accounting is confusing, stay away
  3. 14. "Not too likely" we'll buy a business outside the U.S.
  4. 25. Business schools should study Mrs. B's success
  5. 30. Early Buffett cigar butt: Delta Duck Club
  6. 31. Secret to avoiding lawsuits: "You can't make a good deal with a bad person"

3. Coca-Cola "doing exactly the right thing" with its cash

AUDIENCE MEMBER: Thank you. Second question concerns dividends. Last Friday night, by coincidence, on Louis Rukeyser's weekly television show, the special guest was Philip Carret.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

Now, if you extend that reasoning, could it also be a beneficial policy if Coca-Cola and Gillette stopped paying dividends and utilized the cash in other ways?

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Well, it depends what they could use the â how they would use â utilize the cash, what they could use it for. Those are more focused enterprises than Berkshire, at least in terms of products.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And they â I think â I commend managements that have a wonderful business for utilizing cash in those wonderful businesses, or in businesses that they understand and that will also have wonderful economics, and for getting the rest of the money back to the shareholders.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So, Coca-Cola, in my book, is doing exactly the right thing with its cash when it both â when, A, it uses all the cash that it can, effectively, in the business to expand in new markets and all of that sort of thing.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But then beyond that, it pays a dividend which distributes cash to shareholders, and then it repurchases shares in a big way, which returns cash on a selective basis to shareholders, but in a way that benefits all of them.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So, we â you will benefit from us not paying dividends just as long as we can use the â every dollar we retain â to produce more than a dollar of value, and of market value over time.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Whether we can continue doing that, you know, how long we can continue doing that, I can't promise you, but that is the â thatâs the yardstick by which the decision is made.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And that is the yardstick, I think, by which Coca-Cola's making the decision, too. And I think that they deserve great credit for exercising the discipline to quit when they â using cash â when they've run out of the opportunities to use it well, and then to use it â then to further deploy it advantageously by repurchasing shares.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I think one of the things I admire about my friend, Bill Gates, heâs got 4 1/2 billion of cash in Microsoft, and very few managements can stand having 4 1/2 billion of cash and not doing something unintelligent with it.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

Charlie?

But the limiting factor on that should be that you pay them a market rate as long as you are getting a market rate on capital. But it's harder to measure the market rate on capital in a short period than it is to measure the market rate on compensation.

I mean, it is very hard to pay market rates for ballplayers in Kansas City and still make money running a ball team, where you've got a smaller television market and all of that of the big cities.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

If you have a situation where market rates, you know, exceed the earning capacity of the business, then at some point, capital will flow away from the business.

Sync Video to Paragraph

In the airline industry, which I use as an example, the market rate â most â well, the â in terms of the bigger airlines, people are not being paid market rates, they're being paid contractual rates. Well, you can't blame anybody for that.

If you have a contract that entitles you to X and the current market is a half of X, you're going to hang onto that contract very aggressively. And like I say, you don't blame anybody for that, it's just if you end up in that condition, though, you've got a real problem.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And if you have the same problem that you have if the market is higher than â or a similar problem â the one you have if the market is higher than one that you can sustain in your own business.

Sync Video to Paragraph

5. Buffett on the "real" advantage of being rich

I have a friend whose grandmother used to say that she couldn't understand why people got into envy-jealousy, because it was the only one of the sins that you could never possibly have any fun at. And â (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah, I've commented from time to time that â what's his name? Robin Leach has it all wrong on âLifestyles of the Rich and Famous,â because he's presenting all these wonderful things that will happen to you if you get rich.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But they really aren't that all that wonderful, these fancy houses and boats and all that. The real advantage of being rich, as I explain to people, is that it enables you to hate so effectively.

Sync Video to Paragraph

That if you're terribly rich, you know, and â but your brother or whomever, cousin or somebody, is getting a little more attention in the world or something of the sort, you can hate in a very major way.

Sync Video to Paragraph

You can hire accountants and lawyers to cause him all kinds of trouble. If you're poor, you just snub him at Thanksgiving and don't show up or something of the sort. (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

But I've noticed that these rich people, particularly when they inherit great amounts of money, sooner or later they start â frequently â they get very antagonistic toward siblings, or cousins, or whatever it may be.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And they really can â they can hate in a way that â or get envious in a way that the rest of us really can't really aspire to. So, that's the benefit that hasn't appeared on Robin Leach lately, but I â

Sync Video to Paragraph

But you see that â you see a little of that in the athletic field and the entertainment field, and perhaps even on Wall Street, that making a million dollars a year looks great until this guy that sits next to you that can't possibly be as smart as you is making a million-two. And then the whole world, it turns into a very unfair place. (Laughter)
